$$

$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(200,\frac{{10}^{2}}{20}) \\  & ∼N(200,5).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
Φ(-0.45)=0.3264.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<199) & ≈Φ(-0.45) \\  & =0.3264.\end{aligned}

\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[\\overline{X}] = \\mu,\n$$\n\nand the variance of the sample mean is\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[\\overline{X}] = \\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}.\n$$\n\nPutting all of this together, we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\overline{X} \\sim N\\left(\\mu, \\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}\\right),\n$$\n\nIn other words, the sample mean $\\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\\mu$ and variance 17592186163327 :tutorial/content "Let $X_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_{n}$ be a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population $N(\\mu,\\sigma^2)$ with mean $\\mu$ and variance $\\sigma^2.$ In other words,   \n\n$$\nX_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_{n} \\sim N(\\mu,\\sigma^2).\n$$\n\nIn this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean\n\n$$\n\\overline{X} = \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.\n$$\n\nRecall the following:\n\n- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed. Thus, \n\n$$\nY = \\displaystyle \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n X_i\n$$\n\nis normally distributed.\n\n- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, \n\n$$\n\\overline{X} = \\dfrac1n\\cdot Y\n$$\n\nis normally distributed.\n\nAlso, we previously saw that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, i.e., \n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[\\overline{X}] = \\mu,\n$$\n\nand the variance of the sample mean is\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[\\overline{X}] = \\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}.\n$$\n\nPutting all of this together, we obtain that\n\n$$\n\\overline{X} \\sim N\\left(\\mu, \\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}\\right),\n$$\n\nIn other words, the sample mean $\\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\\mu$ and variance $\\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "14d0c44e-7b46-50e5-800f-e73c03b66e46" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6277 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a485f6ff-48be-57c5-ba9e-77d399d6168c" :step/math-academy-id 38046 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163073}} {:db/id 17592186163327 :tutorial/content "Let $X_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_{n}$ be a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population $N(\\mu,\\sigma^2)$ with mean $\\mu$ and variance $\\sigma^2.$ In other words,   \n\n$$\nX_1, X_2, \\ldots, X_{n} \\sim N(\\mu,\\sigma^2).\n$$\n\nIn this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean\n\n$$\n\\overline{X} = \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.\n$$\n\nRecall the following:\n\n- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed.
